questions.title: Commonest cause of bilateral proptosis in adults
questions.question: The most common cause of bilateral proptosis in adults is:

explanations.A: Correct. Thyroid (Graves) orbitopathy is by far the commonest cause of proptosis in adults, whether unilateral or bilateral, resulting from autoimmune inflammation and swelling of the extraocular muscles and orbital fat. It typically produces bilateral, often asymmetrical, axial proptosis with lid retraction. Hence thyroid orbitopathy is the leading cause of bilateral adult proptosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orbital metastasis is an uncommon cause and is usually unilateral.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orbital lymphoma is much less common and typically presents unilaterally.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A frontal lobe meningioma does not cause proptosis; a sphenoid-wing meningioma may cause unilateral proptosis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify thyroid orbitopathy as the commonest cause of bilateral adult proptosis.

questions.title: Cause that does not produce lagophthalmos
questions.question: Lagophthalmos can occur in all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it does cause lagophthalmos). Facial (7th) nerve palsy weakens orbicularis oculi so the lids cannot close.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the exception: the trigeminal (5th) nerve is sensory to the eye and motor to mastication, and its palsy does not weaken lid closure, so it does not cause lagophthalmos (though corneal anaesthesia may cause neurotrophic keratitis). Lid closure depends on the facial nerve, not the trigeminal. Hence 5th nerve palsy is the odd one out.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it does cause lagophthalmos). Severe proptosis in thyrotoxic exophthalmos prevents the lids from meeting.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it can cause lagophthalmos). A parotid tumour may infiltrate the facial nerve, producing orbicularis weakness and lagophthalmos.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that trigeminal (5th nerve) palsy does not cause lagophthalmos.

questions.title: Management of acute-on-chronic dacryocystitis
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with an acute painful swelling at the medial canthus. She had been treated for chronic dacryocystitis but was reluctant to undergo surgery. What is the most appropriate current management?

options.A: Surgery connecting the sac to the nose

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dacryocystorhinostomy is the definitive treatment but is deferred until the acute infection has settled.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Probing is used for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants and is inappropriate during acute infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Silicone intubation is not the management of an acute infective episode.
explanations.D: Correct. The picture is acute dacryocystitis (an acute-on-chronic flare), and the immediate management is systemic antibiotics together with warm compresses to control the infection. Definitive dacryocystorhinostomy is performed later, once the acute inflammation has resolved. Hence systemic antibiotics are the appropriate current management.

questions.learning_objective: Select systemic antibiotics as the acute management of acute-on-chronic dacryocystitis.

questions.title: Muscle cause of upper eyelid ptosis
questions.question: Upper eyelid ptosis can be caused by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The orbicularis closes the lid, so its paralysis causes lagophthalmos, not ptosis.
explanations.B: Correct. The levator palpebrae superioris elevates the upper lid, so weakness or dehiscence of this muscle or its aponeurosis produces ptosis. Its smooth-muscle partner, Muller's muscle, contributes a small additional amount of elevation. Hence malfunction of the levator palpebrae superioris causes upper-lid ptosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Overaction of the levator would retract, not droop, the lid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior rectus elevates the globe, not the eyelid.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute upper-lid ptosis to levator palpebrae superioris dysfunction.

questions.title: Definition of ectropion
questions.question: Ectropion means:

options.A: Rolling in of the eyelid margin
options.B: Rolling out of the eyelid margin
options.C: Rubbing of the eyelashes against the cornea

explanations.A: Incorrect. Inward rolling of the lid margin describes entropion.
explanations.B: Correct. Ectropion is an outward turning (eversion) of the eyelid margin away from the globe, commonly involutional in the elderly or secondary to facial nerve palsy or cicatrisation. It exposes the palpebral conjunctiva and causes epiphora and exposure keratopathy. Hence ectropion means rolling out of the lid margin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lashes rubbing on the cornea is trichiasis, often a consequence of entropion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Drooping of the upper eyelid is ptosis.

questions.learning_objective: Define ectropion as outward rolling of the eyelid margin.

questions.title: Feature not seen in thyroid ophthalmopathy
questions.question: Thyroid ophthalmopathy can present with all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it does occur). Restrictive myopathy of the extraocular muscles causes diplopia.
explanations.B: Incorrect (it does occur). Orbital muscle and fat swelling produce proptosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it does occur). Exposure from proptosis and lid retraction leads to exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the exception: thyroid eye disease characteristically causes upper-lid RETRACTION and lid lag, which is the opposite of ptosis. The presence of ptosis would suggest another diagnosis such as coexisting myasthenia gravis. Hence ptosis is not a feature of thyroid ophthalmopathy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that thyroid eye disease causes lid retraction, not ptosis.

questions.title: Ocular effect of facial nerve palsy
questions.question: Facial nerve palsy:

options.C: Causes miosis and loss of eye sensation

explanations.A: Correct. The facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi, so its palsy weakens lid closure, producing lagophthalmos and exposure of the cornea. The exposed cornea is then at risk of drying, ulceration and neurotrophic damage. Hence facial nerve palsy causes lagophthalmos and corneal exposure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ptosis with a 'down-and-out' eye characterises a third (oculomotor) nerve palsy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Miosis is seen in Horner's syndrome, and corneal sensation is carried by the trigeminal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Facial palsy does not directly reduce vision unless exposure keratopathy supervenes.

questions.learning_objective: State that facial nerve palsy causes lagophthalmos and corneal exposure.

questions.title: Definition of entropion
questions.question: Entropion is:

options.A: Rolling in of the lid margin
options.C: Downward drooping of the upper lid
options.D: Outward protrusion of the lower lid

explanations.A: Correct. Entropion is an inward turning (inversion) of the eyelid margin so that the lashes rub against the cornea and conjunctiva. It is commonly involutional or cicatricial (for example after trachoma) and causes irritation and corneal damage from the resulting trichiasis. Hence entropion is rolling in of the lid margin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An accessory row of lashes is distichiasis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Downward drooping of the upper lid is ptosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Outward turning of the lid margin is ectropion.

questions.learning_objective: Define entropion as inward rolling of the eyelid margin.

questions.title: Standard treatment of chronic dacryocystitis in adults
questions.question: The standard procedure for the treatment of chronic dacryocystitis in adults is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Probing is used for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in infants.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Silicone intubation is an adjunct rather than the standard adult procedure.
explanations.C: Correct. Chronic dacryocystitis in adults results from nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and the definitive treatment is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), which creates a new drainage passage between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity. This bypasses the blocked duct and relieves the stagnation and recurrent infection. Hence DCR is the standard procedure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sac massage is used in congenital cases, not adult chronic dacryocystitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify dacryocystorhinostomy as the standard treatment of adult chronic dacryocystitis.

questions.title: Term for incomplete lid closure
questions.question: Incomplete closure of the palpebral fissure when the eyelids are shut is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eyelids completely, leaving part of the palpebral fissure open when closure is attempted. It results from facial nerve palsy, severe proptosis or lid scarring, and predisposes to exposure keratopathy. Hence incomplete lid closure is called lagophthalmos.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ptosis is drooping of the upper eyelid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bell's phenomenon is the protective upward rolling of the globe on attempted lid closure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Blepharochalasis is recurrent lid oedema leaving lax, redundant lid skin.

questions.learning_objective: Name incomplete palpebral closure as lagophthalmos.

questions.title: Features of ulcerative blepharitis
questions.question: In ulcerative blepharitis:

options.A: The lid margin is not inflamed.
options.B: Scaly dandruff-like material is seen between the cilia.
options.D: There are yellow crusts and ulcers on the lid margin.

explanations.A: Incorrect. In ulcerative blepharitis the lid margin is inflamed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Scaly dandruff-like material describes squamous (seborrhoeic) blepharitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ulcerative blepharitis is staphylococcal and is treated with antibiotics and lid hygiene, not antifungals.
explanations.D: Correct. Ulcerative (staphylococcal) blepharitis is characterised by hard yellow crusts at the lash bases which, when removed, reveal small bleeding ulcers on an inflamed lid margin. Chronic disease leads to lash loss, trichiasis and lid-margin scarring. Hence yellow crusts and ulcers on the lid margin typify ulcerative blepharitis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the yellow crusts and marginal ulcers of ulcerative blepharitis.

questions.title: Cause not associated with ptosis
questions.question: The well-known causes of ptosis include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (it is a cause). Blunt trauma can disinsert the levator aponeurosis, producing aponeurotic ptosis.
explanations.B: Correct. This is the exception: systemic hypertension is not a recognised cause of ptosis. The genuine causes are neurogenic (third-nerve palsy, Horner's syndrome), myogenic (myasthenia, myopathies), aponeurotic (age, trauma) and mechanical. Hence hypertension is the odd one out.
explanations.C: Incorrect (it is a cause). Fatigable ptosis is a classic feature of myasthenia gravis.
explanations.D: Incorrect (it is a cause). Loss of Muller's-muscle tone in Horner's syndrome gives a mild ptosis.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that hypertension is not a cause of ptosis.
